chapter: Louis Armstrong, Gene Krupa and the drum school
title: Armstrong repertoire and drumming

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: You said that obviously you were doing some of the traditional Dixieland tunes.
But you did a lot of other things as well, right?
Oh yeah. It was not only Dixieland we played, we played a lot of Earl's tunes, "Rosetta," "Monday Date," all those things, Earl's tunes, Louie's tunes, Louie's wasn't all Dixieland.
Sure. Some of those things he probably hadn't played that much even in his prime, when he was, you know the Hot Five and Hot Seven days, he hadn't played those.
Yeah, that's right. So Louie had a good repertoire, all different tunes, swing tunes, good Dixieland tunes. Well all of Louie's tunes, even the Dixieland tunes were swinging.
Yah, you were basically playing more or less
a four-four type drumming...... you weren't playing like...

No, no I wasn't playing that. Some of the beats I would put in would be the traditional beat you know. But I'd keep them, maybe if it sound good with a two beat, do that, if it sound good with four, do that, but they'd always know that it was a Dixieland tune and it'd be swinging, you know.

Sure. There are I guess a lot of guys were playing maybe even with the three horn front line but who were like people who came up in the '30s and '40s like Roy Eldridge and ... that's what Roy Eldridge does now at Jimmy Ryan's you know, you know he does some of those tunes, but you know, it's not really Dixieland.
Oh no, no. Roy does it his ways and swings them.
